title: Unborn, beyond the elements
hook: ajoo hain, abhoo hain: never born, not made of earth or water (Jaap, chachari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, formless: aroop hain, anoop hain, and your line, beyond compare. Today, the next two short lines of the chachari.

Everything you've ever touched was made of something. The table: wood, which was a tree, which was soil and rain and light. Your coffee: water, beans, heat. Your own body: about sixty percent water, plus minerals that were once in the ground, plus the air in your lungs right now. Even you had a birthday: a day, a place, a mother. Everything has a when it began and a what it's made of. Jaap Sahib names something that has neither.
screen: `THE TABLE WAS A TREE.` → `YOUR BODY: WATER, MINERALS, AIR.` → `EVERYTHING HAS A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: The two-word lines keep coming. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. Joon is a Punjabi word for a birth, a life-form, a body you're born into. Ajoo, and its fuller form ajooni, means never born into any form. If that sounds familiar, it should. It's in the Mool Mantar, Guru Nanak's words that open the Guru Granth Sahib, the lines many Sikhs learn first: ajooni saibhang, unborn, self-existent. Guru Arjan set them at the head of the scripture when he compiled it in 1604, and here the Tenth Guru brings the idea back, nearly two centuries after Guru Nanak, in his own morning praise. The first Guru and the tenth, saying the same thing in different meters. Then abhoo. Bhoo is the earth, the stuff things are made of; abhoo, not made of earth. Sikh scripture often speaks of the body as made of five elements, earth, water, fire, air and space, borrowed for a while and given back. The One, Jaap says, isn't made of any of them. Not a very large person, not a force inside the world like gravity, but something not built from the world's materials at all. Sikh teaching holds firmly that the One is never born and never dies. On an ordinary day, that matters. Everything you can touch will change, wear out and return to the ground, your own hands included. That can be frightening. Ajooni says that what you bow to is not on that list. Not made of this, so it can't wear out.
screen: `JOON: A BIRTH, A BODY.` · `AJOONI: NEVER BORN.` · `MOOL MANTAR: AJOONI SAIBHANG.` · `ABHOO: NOT MADE OF EARTH.` · then, large: `NOT MADE OF THIS.`

segments.voice: Put your fingers on something solid, soil, a stone, the floor, then on something wet, a glass of water or a damp cloth: both made, and your hand is made of them too. Now rest your hand in your lap and let your attention go past what you can touch, to the quiet behind it. If you pray, you can say ajooni softly.
Ajooni. Never born into any body: the word from the Mool Mantar that Jaap echoes with ajoo hain, abhoo hain, unborn and not made of earth.
Your line: not made of this. Whatever wears out, the One you bow to doesn't. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 340 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SALUTATION TO THE ARMED ONE.`

fork.setup: the Tenth Guru is writing his morning praise. which earlier Sikh words does he echo in ajoo hain?
options: a line from a Persian poem.
fork.reveal: Guru Nanak's opening lines call the One ajooni, unborn; the Tenth Guru brings it back nearly two centuries later.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ajooni, never born into any body, from joon, a birth; in the Mool Mantar.

what a scholar hears: ajoo and abhoo in Jaap's chachari restate the Mool Mantar's ajooni saibhang; joon comes from Sanskrit yoni, birth or womb.

chat.says: Was God born at some point, like everything else, just a very long time ago?
options: No: Jaap says ajoo, never born, like the Mool Mantar's ajooni, and not made of earth either.
Yes, God was born first of all, before the earth, which is why God is so old.
God is made of the finest earth and water, so God never wears out like we do.
chat.meaning: Ajoo hain echoes the Mool Mantar's ajooni, never born; abhoo hain says the One isn't made of earth or any element.

notes: Ajoo glossed as unborn and abhoo as not made of earth/elements; some translations render abhoo differently (e.g., 'without elements', 'not of the world'). Confirm.
Five elements (earth, water, fire, air, space/akash) as a Gurbani theme: confirm.
'A little over two centuries later' (Guru Nanak's Mool Mantar to Jaap, late 1600s): confirm.
Body water 'about sixty percent' is an approximate adult figure.
